I recently completed my Software Development Engineer Internship at Amazon Web Services (AWS) , where I worked on the Amazon Athena team! Over the summer, I had the opportunity to build operational tooling for investigating complex workloads. I: • Built an operations console that aggregated and streamed Spark workload state, giving on-call engineers a unified view during investigations. • Designed private connectivity for console diagnostics using Amazon VPC networking and Route 53 private DNS. • Built a diagnostic agent that surfaced likely failure causes and reduced the manual work required during incident diagnosis. Along the way, I learned a great deal about cloud infrastructure, operational reliability, and the scale and complexity at which AWS systems operate. Beyond the technical work, I enjoyed learning how the team approached real on-call challenges, sharing team lunches, and getting to know the people who made the experience so memorable. A huge thank you to Sophia Tsang, Gaurav Agrawal , and Shubham Mehta for their guidance, thoughtful feedback, and mentorship throughout my internship. I’m also grateful to the entire team for making the experience so rewarding. I’m excited to bring everything I learned back to Purdue and into whatever I build next! #Amazon #AWS #SoftwareEngineering #CloudInfrastructure

What happens when you put 500 autonomous agents in a world with limited food, money, energy and health — and let them figure out how to survive? Over the past few weeks, I’ve been building Agent World, a multi-agent simulation to learn reinforcement learning from the ground up. Each agent lives for up to 1,200 simulated days and has four possible actions: work, rest, buy food, or form an alliance. Every decision has a tradeoff. Working earns money, but consumes food and energy. Buying food helps survival, but costs money. Resting restores the agent, but sacrifices an opportunity to earn. Agents can also trade with others, remember previous interactions, and form alliances. I initially built the learning system using tabular Q-learning. But as the state space became more complex, I wanted the agents to generalize rather than simply memorize state-action combinations. So I replaced the Q-table with a neural network and gradually built out a Deep Q-Network (DQN) — implementing each component individually so I could understand why it was necessary: → Neural Q-function approximation → ε-greedy exploration → Experience replay → Mini-batch training → Bellman targets → Terminal-state handling → A separate target network with periodic synchronization One of my favorite realizations while building this was that the agents themselves effectively create the training dataset by living. 500 agents × 1,200 days can generate up to 600,000 experiences in a single episode. Those experiences enter a replay buffer, random batches are sampled, and the shared neural network continuously updates its weights based on what worked — and what very much did not. The interesting part now is no longer getting the DQN to run. It’s figuring out what it actually learns. Does survival improve across episodes? Does it learn when sacrificing wealth for food is worthwhile? Does cooperation become strategically useful? What happens to wealth inequality? And perhaps most importantly: does the behavior I want actually match the reward function I designed? That last question has already been one of the biggest lessons from this project: An RL agent doesn't optimize what you intended. It optimizes what you rewarded. Now moving into longer training runs, reward-function tuning, and evaluating the trained policy against baseline strategies. Code + full technical breakdown on GitHub: https://lnkd.in/dQ-sg_N5 #ReinforcementLearning #DeepLearning #MachineLearning #PyTorch #DQN #ArtificialIntelligence

Should you chase hype or ignore it? The tech industry has been debating this for decades. So Sequoia Capital , we dug into 20 years of hype data. This summer, I worked with Sequoia intern Oliver Cho to measure hype over the past 2 decades. The chart below ranks the most hyped topics on Hacker News for every year since 2007. Under each year sits the most valuable company founded that year. Here are a few observations: 1/ The top company founded in a given year is rarely related to the hype of that period. Airbnb was founded in 2008, when the top topic was Google. Uber arrived in 2009, while the conversation revolved around low-level programming. Anthropic came in 2021, while the internet was consumed by crypto. Chasing hype rarely leads to enduring outcomes. The top companies of recent years have yet to be decided. 2/ New trends announce themselves five to six years early. LLMs first cracked the top 15 in 2016 and took until 2022 to hit #1. AI coding entered at #12 in 2021 and tops the list in 2026. Crypto entered in 2011 before 2017 and 2021 peaks. “New” trends don’t appear out of nowhere, and internet subcommunities are often the first to know where the puck is headed. 3/ Long-term “hype” is a durable signal. The “Musk-Verse” has been a top 15 topic for every one of the past 14 years. Sustained attention on the internet is rare and tends to mark something real. Next up, we want to run the same analysis with sources like X and LinkedIn. If that's of interest, give us some encouragement and we'll share the results.
